title: The Church's clock
hookLine: psalms prayed at set hours around the world by priests, religious and laypeople

lines: A PRIEST AT HIS KITCHEN TABLE.
cards: Right now, as you listen, somewhere on earth it's early morning, and in a monastery chapel a few sleepy monks are standing up to sing a psalm.

Somewhere else it's evening, and a parish priest is opening a worn book at his kitchen table. Somewhere else a nurse on a night shift is reading the same psalm on her phone during her break. They've never met.
They're praying the same words, set for the same day, on the same clock. The Church has a name for that clock.

teach.h: SEVEN TIMES A DAY: OLDER THAN THE CHURCH.
teach.b: First, the roots. Praying at set times of day is older than Christianity. The psalmist says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Seven times a day I have given praise to thee."
The book of Daniel describes him praying three times a day toward Jerusalem. In Acts, Peter and John go up to the Temple at the ninth hour of prayer. The apostles kept the rhythm.
Second, the monks. Saint Benedict's Rule builds the monks' day around these hours and sets out the whole psalter, all one hundred fifty psalms, every week.
Benedict called it the work of God, and nothing, he said, was to be put before it. Over time it was prayed above all by monks, nuns and clergy, and called the Divine Office. Third, the hours today.

After the Second Vatican Council it was reshaped and published under the title Liturgy of the Hours, though many still call it the Divine Office, and the Church urged laypeople to pray it too, especially morning and evening prayer.

The main hours: the Office of Readings, Morning Prayer, Daytime Prayer, Evening Prayer, and Night Prayer, which is tomorrow. Priests and deacons promise to pray it every day, and religious communities pray it too.
Each hour is mostly psalms, with a short reading, a hymn and prayers. Fourth, the clock.
The Church spans every time zone, so as one place finishes evening prayer, another is beginning morning prayer.

teach.h: SEVEN TIMES A DAY I HAVE GIVEN PRAISE TO THEE.
teach.b: The idea is that the whole Church, together, keeps the day holy, hour by hour. Catholics say no one prays it alone, even when they're alone.

how: Catholic priests, deacons and many religious pray the Liturgy of the Hours daily, and laypeople pray morning and evening prayer from a breviary or an app, alone or in parishes.

games.q: you're a monk living under Saint Benedict's Rule. the bell rings for one of the hours while you're halfway through a job. what does the Rule say?
o: drop it and go: nothing is put before the work of God.
games.why: Benedict's Rule says that nothing is to be put before the work of God, the hours of prayer.

practice: Evening prayer uses a line from Psalm 140: let my prayer be directed as incense in thy sight; the lifting up of my hands, as evening sacrifice. Say it slowly, picturing the smoke of incense rising in a dark church and hands lifted.
If you pray, pray it; if you don't, read it knowing others are reading it too.

wordCard.voice: Divine Office. The Church's older name for its daily round of psalms at set hours, prayed by monks, clergy and now laypeople around the world. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: the Liturgy of the Hours, the name given after Vatican II.

carryVoice: Your line: someone is always praying. Even when you feel alone, somewhere a psalm is being prayed. Until tomorrow.
